title: OAuth PKCE
summary: PKCE binds an OAuth authorization code to a secret generated for that authorization attempt.
overview: The client sends an S256 challenge derived from a fresh random verifier in the authorization request. At token exchange, the server checks the supplied verifier against that challenge before issuing tokens.
why: An intercepted authorization code alone should not let an attacker obtain tokens.
example: A mobile app retains a verifier during browser authorization, then submits it with the returned code to the token endpoint.
judgment: Choose a maintained OAuth library and verify redirect handling, transaction binding, and verifier protection; PKCE does not replace authorization policy.
next: Does our authorization server reject a token exchange with a missing or incorrect verifier?
